newsitem.title: USA: Virginia governor commutes killer's death sentence.
newsitem.headline: Virginia governor commutes killer's death sentence.

text.p: Virginia Gov. George Allen commuted the death sentence of twice-convicted killer Joseph Patrick Payne on Thursday, hours before he was scheduled to die for the slaying of a fellow prison inmate.

Allen commuted the death sentence to life in prison without possibility of parole. Payne had been scheduled to die via lethal injection at 9 p.m. EST on Thursday (0200 GMT on Friday) for the 1985 killing of David Wayne Dunford.

Payne's lawyers had asked for clemency for their client based on a plea from Dunford's mother and purported new evidence that had caused several of the jurors who recommended the death sentence for Payne to change their minds.

But Allen, who said there was "ample" evidence of Payne's guilt, decided to commute the death sentence based on the "totality of the records, evidence and materials before me" and not because of the wavering jurors.

"I am not commuting Payne's sentence of death based on any consideration whatsoever of the affidavits purporting to be recently obtained 'second thoughts' by a few jurors," Allen said in a statement. "I have not given any weight or credence to those affidavits."
Allen, a conservative Republican who won office by promising to get tough on crime, has allowed 10 executions to proceed since he took office in 1994.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday voted 7-2 to deny Payne's request for a stay of execution. The high court said only that Justices John Paul Stevens and Ruth Bader Ginsburg would grant the application.

Payne was convicted and sentenced to die for the March 3, 1985, slaying of Dunford, 28, who was serving a 15-year sentence for auto theft at the Powhatan Correctional Centre near Richmond. Dunford was set on fire in his cell and died nine days later without identifying his killer.

At the time of Dunford's slaying, Payne was serving a life sentence at Powhatan for the 1981 capital murder of grocery store owner Louise Winslow in Bristow, Virginia. He shot Winslow during a robbery as his three-year-old son sat outside in the escape vehicle.

In an affidavit signed Oct. 29 and sent to the governor as part of Payne's clemency petition, Dunford's mother, Reba Dunford, said, "I have doubts that Joe Payne killed my son. I can think of no greater tragedy than killing an innocent man. Please do not let this happen, Gov. Allen. It would be a terrible mistake and one that I could not live with."

Witnesses at Payne's trial were prison inmates, and the key testimony came from inmate Robert Francis "Dirty Smitty" Smith. Smith was the only man who claimed to have witnessed Dunford's slaying and he fingered Payne as the killer.
But another inmate testified that he saw Payne in the shower at the time that Dunford was set on fire.

The jury accepted Smith's testimony, and did not learn that he later recanted his testimony and then changed his story again, nor did they hear that other inmates had come forward after the trial to say Payne was innocent.

"I can't begin to say how heavily this has weighed on me," said juror Shelly Brydie Gray in an affidavit. "I have often thought that this mistake would be something I would have to one day settle with God."
Payne would have been the 33rd inmate put to death in Virginia since the 1977 resumption of the death penalty. Only Texas and Florida have executed more prisoners.
The Washington, D.C.-based Death Penalty Information Centre said a governor had commuted a death sentence 35 times since the reinstatement of capital punishment.
